block.semiconductor-lab.test_power_sourc: A block for checking the game, not normally obtainable. It gives electricity forever without fuel.

Creative only, no recipe. Placed under (next to) a machine it sends 1 MW. The test site (/function semiconductor-lab:testworld) puts one under each machine. Check real power generation in the test site's steam engine area.

In the real world there is no power source that needs no fuel: electricity is converted from the energy of fuel, flowing water, light and so on (conservation of energy). This block is just a shortcut for testing.
Labs often test a device on a regulated bench power supply instead of its real power source. The test site uses the same idea.
For testing only: not a real technology (just for checking the game).

litho.semiconductor-lab.discovery.diffus: A thin diffused strip resists current: a resistor. Kilby's first IC of 1958 (germanium) already had resistors made from the wafer itself.
litho.semiconductor-lab.discovery.juncti: The border between p-type and n-type lets current through one way only. In 1940 Ohl found such a border by chance inside a silicon crystal.
litho.semiconductor-lab.discovery.planar: Open windows in the oxide and diffuse n, p, n nested inside each other: a transistor. Hoerni's 1959 method keeps the surface flat.
litho.semiconductor-lab.discovery.rtl_no: A circuit of just a transistor and resistors that outputs 0 for input 1 and 1 for input 0 (RTL). One of the logic circuits announced as ICs in 1961.
Inventions from history hide in the chips you draw. Press Probe at the probe station.

block.semiconductor-lab.surface_plate.no: A perfectly flat iron table, the reference for measuring flatness and length.
Cast iron plates lapped three together until the warp is 1 um or less. It can be placed. Lapping it again against a warped plate can warp it again.
Inspection rooms still have cast iron or granite surface plates. In the 20th century granite, which does not rust and moves little with temperature, became common.
Precise measuring and assembly begin on a surface plate. Gauge blocks ([8-05]) and isolation tables ([8-07]) only make sense once there is a flat reference.
tooltip.semiconductor-lab.oxygen.cz: Oxygen about %s ppma (CZ: from the quartz crucible)
litho.semiconductor-lab.discovery.monoli: A transistor and a separate resistor on one silicon chip, joined by aluminium wiring laid on the oxide. Noyce (Fairchild) wrote this idea down in 1959. Kilby's IC of 1958 was germanium, with its parts joined by thin gold wires in the air: the first IC, but not flat and hard to make in numbers.

litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.and.go: Light up only when both A and B get power
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.xor.go: Output 1 when exactly one of A and B gets power

litho.semiconductor-lab.near.roles: Hint: set the pads first - 0 V, 5 V, the inputs and the output.
litho.semiconductor-lab.near.no_current: Hint: no current flows from 5 V. Is something between 5 V and 0 V, and are they wired?
litho.semiconductor-lab.near.no_switch: Hint: current flows, but nothing works as a switch yet (no transistor).
litho.semiconductor-lab.near.almost_tran: Hint: almost a transistor - one region has no wire yet.
litho.semiconductor-lab.near.input_not_b: Hint: an input does not reach the base of any transistor.

litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.self: You found %s on your own, without hints!
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.not.hi: ① When the input is 5 V, something must pull the output down to 0 V.
② A transistor is a switch: power on the base lets current through from collector to emitter.
③ Collector to 5 V through a resistor, emitter to 0 V, input to the base through a resistor; the output is the collector.
④ This is the RTL inverter, a part of Fairchild's Micrologic family (1961).
This is the same circuit as the RTL inverter of Fairchild's Micrologic (1961).
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.nor.hi: ① If either input has power, the output must go to 0 V.
② Two switches side by side: either one can pull the output down.
③ Two NOT circuits whose collectors are joined, with one resistor to 5 V.
④ The RTL NOR gate: Micrologic (1961) built logic from it, and the Apollo Guidance Computer used thousands of NOR-gate ICs.
This is the same circuit as the RTL NOR gate of Micrologic (1961), the gate the Apollo Guidance Computer was built from.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.or.hin: ① Output 1 if A or B has power.
② OR is the opposite of NOR.
③ A NOR followed by a NOT.
④ In RTL, OR was built as NOR + NOT: one kind of gate was made into everything.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.or.his: OR from NOR + NOT: how RTL designers of the early 1960s made every function from one gate.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.nand.h: ① Only when both inputs have power does the output go to 0 V.
② Two switches in a row (in series): current passes only if both are on.
③ Two transistors stacked: the top collector to 5 V through a resistor (the output), the bottom emitter to 0 V.
④ NAND became the workhorse of DTL and TTL logic in the 1960s. ⚠️ exact first-product years are not confirmed.
NAND: the gate of 1960s DTL and TTL logic. ⚠️ years not confirmed.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.and.hi: ① Light only when both A and B have power.
② AND is the opposite of NAND.
③ A NAND followed by a NOT (or: NOT each input, then NOR).
④ De Morgan's law (1847): A AND B = NOT(NOT A OR NOT B). Every gate can be made from NAND alone, or from NOR alone.
AND: De Morgan (1847) showed it can be built from the opposite gates.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.xor.hi: ① Output 1 when exactly one input has power.
② XOR = (A OR B) AND NOT (A AND B).
③ Four NAND gates make an XOR.
④ XOR is the 'sum' bit of binary addition: 1+1 = 10, so the sum digit is 0.
XOR: the sum bit of binary addition.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.half_a: ① Add two 1-bit numbers: output 1 = sum digit, output 2 = carry.
③ Put an XOR and an AND side by side, sharing the inputs A and B.
④ In 1937 George Stibitz built a 1-bit binary adder from telephone relays on his kitchen table (the 'Model K').
A half adder: the same job as Stibitz's relay 'Model K' of 1937, now on one chip.
Challenges solved without opening any hint.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.full_a: Add A, B and the carry-in C: output 1 = sum, output 2 = carry-out
① Three 1-bit numbers in, a 2-bit answer out: 1+1+1 = 11.
② Two half adders in a row, plus an OR for the two carries.
③ sum = A XOR B XOR C; carry = (A AND B) OR (C AND (A XOR B)). Too big for 16x16: build it from stamps on a stepper grid (24 or more).

④ Chain 4 full adders and you have a 4-bit adder, like the 1960s TTL chips. ⚠️ the exact part and year are not confirmed. In 1971 calculator chips (Busicom and Intel's 4004) did their adding with circuits like this.
A full adder: chain four and you have the 4-bit adder of 1960s TTL logic, the step before the 1971 calculator chips. ⚠️ part numbers and years not confirmed.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.sr_lat: Remember a bit: input A (set) makes output 1 high, input B (reset) makes it low, and with both off it keeps what it had
The same idea as the Eccles-Jordan flip-flop of 1918 (two vacuum tubes), now two transistors on one chip.
① The output must stay the same after the input that changed it goes away.
② Feed each gate's output back into the other: two NORs that hold each other.
③ NOR1(S, Q) gives not-Q; NOR2(R, not-Q) gives Q. With RTL, two transistors whose collectors drive each other's bases through resistors.
④ This is the Eccles-Jordan 'trigger circuit' of 1918, first built with two vacuum tubes: the flip-flop.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.d_latc: While the clock is on, output 1 copies input A (D); when the clock goes off, it keeps the last value
A D latch: the building block of registers and early memories.
① Only listen to D while the clock is on.
② An SR latch plus a gate: set = D AND clock, reset = NOT D AND clock.
③ Build the gates from your NOR/NOT stamps and feed them into an SR latch stamp.
④ Latches like this hold each bit in early IC memories and registers. ⚠️ product names and years not confirmed.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.counte: Count clock pulses 0, 1, 2, 3, 0 on outputs 1 (low bit) and 2 (high bit); input A resets to 0
A counter: the same job as Wynn-Williams's scale-of-two counter of 1932, now in transistors.
① The low bit flips on every clock pulse; the high bit flips when the low bit goes from 1 to 0.
② A flip-flop that toggles (T flip-flop) halves the frequency. Two in a chain count to 4.
③ Make a toggle from two D latches (master and slave) with not-Q fed back to D, then connect the low bit's output to the high bit's clock (ripple counter).
④ In 1932 Wynn-Williams counted particles with a 'scale-of-two' counter of thyratron tubes, the ancestor of every digital counter.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.regist: When the clock rises, outputs 1 and 2 take inputs A and B; the rest of the time they keep their values
A register: CPUs keep numbers in rows of these; the 4004 of 1971 had sixteen 4-bit registers.
① Two memories that only change when the clock rises.
② One edge-triggered flip-flop per bit, all sharing one clock.
③ Stamp the same flip-flop twice and join their clock inputs; use symbols to keep the wiring readable.
④ A CPU is mostly registers and adders. The Intel 4004 (1971) held its numbers in sixteen 4-bit registers.
item.semiconductor-lab.mirror.tarnish.sp: Speculum: oxidises and sulfides within weeks; needs re-polishing
item.semiconductor-lab.mirror.tarnish.si: Silver: yellows and blackens within months from sulfur in the air (silver sulfide); needs re-silvering
item.semiconductor-lab.mirror.tarnish.al: Aluminium: a few-nm oxide film forms and stops further corrosion. Stays bright for years
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.dram_c: A (write) stores B (data); C (read) shows the opposite on output 1. It may leak away, but a rewrite (refresh) keeps it
Intel 1103 (1970): the first DRAM to sell (1 kbit, three-transistor cell). Dennard's one transistor plus one capacitor (1968) later took over.
1. You store an amount of charge. A MOS gate passes no current, so it can hold charge.
2. Three MOSFETs: a gate that lets data in on write, a MOSFET whose gate is the stored charge, and a gate that opens on read.
3. Pull the read line up to the supply through a resistor; put the storage and read MOSFETs in series to 0 V. A stored 1 pulls the line low (inverted).
4. Charge leaks away in a few ms, faster on a dirty chip. A wider gate, or a capacitor (metal over gate oxide on an n region), holds it longer.
block.semiconductor-lab.inverter.note1: Turns direct current into alternating current by switching it rapidly with semiconductor switches.
block.semiconductor-lab.inverter.note2: Back face = DC input, front face = AC output (same voltage class). 95% efficient. Lets solar cells and batteries feed transformers and AC networks. ⚠️ Keep the front and back on separate cable networks (on one network everything becomes AC and DC machines stop).
block.semiconductor-lab.inverter.note3: Switches on and off hundreds or thousands of times a second, flipping the direction to shape AC (the reverse of a rectifier). Changing the AC frequency changes how fast an AC motor turns.
block.semiconductor-lab.inverter.note4: First built with thyristors, then from the 1980s with power MOSFETs and IGBTs ⚠️ (date being checked). Electric cars, air conditioners and trains switch power thousands of times a second to drive their motors.
block.semiconductor-lab.inverter.placeho: Omitted: ⚠️ frequency and motor speed are not modelled. Efficiency is a game value.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.cpu4.g: A-D: ROM word in, 5-8: address out, 1-4: output port. Build a CPU running LOAD, ADD, OUT, JUMP
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.cpu4.h: Intel 4004 (1971): about 2,300 transistors, 10 um, 46 instructions, made for Busicom's calculator by Shima, Faggin, Hoff and Mazor.
1. One word per clock: the first goes into the instruction register, the second is executed. A counter's low bit tells which.
2. The address always adds 1 (half adders), except on JUMP. Choose with NOT, AND and OR (a multiplexer).
3. A takes the number on LOAD, A + number on ADD (four full adders). Split the clock with AND so registers store only then.
4. Build only from stamps with wires between (checked as logic boxes). About 50 stamps; two metal layers keep wires from crossing.
litho.semiconductor-lab.near.program: A CPU is checked as logic: only passed stamps and wires. Something is drawn outside the stamps, or it behaves differently.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.rom_pr: A, B, C = address (A is the low bit); outputs 1-4 give that word: 1,3,2,5,4,0,8,6 (the 3 + 5 program)
Intel 4001 (1971): the program ROM (256 words of 8 bits), written in the factory by one mask.
1. Decode the address: make lines that select exactly one of the 8 words (a NOR pulled low by any wrong address bit).
2. You need the opposite of each address bit too (NOT). Put a gate under the wrong one of each pair.
3. Run data lines down, pulled up to the supply. A MOS where a word line crosses makes that bit 0; none makes it 1.
4. Only the gate-oxide mask decides the contents. Each 4001 customer got that one mask redrawn.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.mcu4.g: Put a CPU and a ROM on one chip. With only the clock as input, show the built-in program's answer (3 + 5) on outputs 1-4
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.mcu4.h: TI TMS1000 (1974): CPU, ROM, RAM and I/O on one chip. It went inside calculators, toys and microwave ovens.
1. Press your passed CPU (cpu4) and ROM (rom_program) stamps on the same sheet.
2. Wire the CPU's address (outputs 5-7) to the ROM's inputs A-C, and the ROM's word (outputs 1-4) to the CPU's inputs A-D.
3. Only the supply, 0 V, clock and output port leave the chip. No outside ROM any more.
4. The real TMS1000 held a 1024-word program and did the same job inside appliances for years.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.cpu8.g: A-H: 8-bit ROM word in, 9-12: address out, 1-8: output port. Run 100 + 55 and counting past 15
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.cpu8.h: Intel 8008 (1972): the first 8-bit CPU (about 3,500 transistors). The 8080 (1974) led to the personal computer (Altair, 1975).
1. Same shape as the 4-bit CPU, with A, the output port, the adders and the choosers doubled to 8 bits. The address stays 4 bits.
2. Chain eight full adders, carry rippling from the low bit up.
3. The instruction only needs the low 4 bits of the word (LOAD, ADD, OUT, JUMP).
4. 8 bits hold 0-255. One character (ASCII) is 8 bits too: computers could now handle text.
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.mul4.g: A-D = x, E-H = y (low bit first). Build a circuit that puts x * y (0-225) on outputs 1-8. A part of the AI chip
litho.semiconductor-lab.challenge.mul4.h: Multiplying is repeated adding. An AI chip (Google's TPU, 2016) lays out 256 x 256 8-bit multipliers to do a neural network's multiply-adds at once.
1. x * y: for each bit of y, copy x or not (AND), shift, and add.
2. Sixteen ANDs make the partial products: x_i AND y_j goes to the 2^(i+j) place.
3. Add one row at a time with four full adders (three rows = 12). Carries go to the next place.
4. Line up many of these and the AI's multiply-adds run faster. The count is speed; the challenge proves it is right.

block.semiconductor-lab.robot_arm.note1: An arm that repeats what you teach it: take from this machine, put into that one.
block.semiconductor-lab.robot_arm.note2: Right-click the arm with a teach pendant, then the machine to take from, then the machine to put into. Within 3 blocks, once a second, up to 16 items. It remembers 1 move, or 8 with your own microcomputer inside.
block.semiconductor-lab.robot_arm.note3: In 1961 the first industrial robot, Unimate, went into an American car plant. Its first job was pulling hot metal parts out of a die-casting machine, work that was dangerous for people.
block.semiconductor-lab.robot_arm.note4: Devol filed a patent for an arm that repeats taught motions in 1954 (granted 1961). The arm moved by oil pressure and stored its steps on a magnetic drum. Japan built them from 1969, and in 1977 a robot with every joint driven by electric motors appeared.
block.semiconductor-lab.robot_arm.placeh: Simplified: the real arm was hydraulic and stored steps on a magnetic drum (the game uses 1 kW and remembers only moves)

block.semiconductor-lab.oht_rail.note1: A rail on the factory ceiling. Carriages run along it carrying wafer boxes (FOUPs).
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_rail.note2: Crafting: 3 steel → 8. Joins to neighbours (up and down too). A load port up to 4 blocks below a dead end is a drop-off point. The rail glows where the carriage is.
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_rail.note3: In today's 300 mm fabs kilometres of ceiling rail carry FOUPs between tools on hundreds of carriages; people hardly carry wafers at all ⚠️.
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_rail.note4: A FOUP weighs about 8 kg; carrying them all day is hard and a drop ruins 25 wafers. So 300 mm fabs were built with automated transport from the start ⚠️.
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_rail.howto: Run it along the ceiling from a drive. A load port up to 4 blocks below a dead end is a drop-off point. It glows where the carriage is.
block.minecraft.furnace.note1: A fire walled in with stone. Heat bounces off the walls, so it gets hotter than a campfire (about 1000 °C).
block.minecraft.furnace.note2: In this mod it is a ~1000 °C furnace. Silver (962 °C) and germanium (938 °C) melt, but above copper (1085 °C) you need bellows ([3-04]) or a hotter furnace. An optical pyrometer can read it.
block.minecraft.furnace.note3: Walling in a fire sends its radiated heat back from the walls, so heat builds up inside. The ancestor of pottery kilns and smithing hearths.
block.minecraft.furnace.note4: Pottery kilns were in use in West Asia about 8,000 years ago ⚠️. Smelting copper and iron ores in it is kept as an approximation of the bloomery and crucible furnace (real ones work at about 1100–1200 °C).
block.minecraft.furnace.placeholder: Approximation: ⚠️ the furnace is fixed at about 1000 °C. Ore smelting stands in for the bloomery and crucible furnace.
